cards.text: Then the LORD speaks to Moses and Aaron. He's laying out what happens when someone gets a swelling, a rash or a bright spot on their skin that may be an infectious skin disease. No doctor's office here, friend. That person gets brought to Aaron the priest or one of his sons who is a priest.
The priest leans in and examines the spot. He's checking two things: the hair in it, and how deep the sore goes.

cards.question: The priest finds the hair in the spot has turned white, and the sore looks deeper than the skin. What does he do?

answers.text: He shaves the spot and waits
He sends the person to wash in the river

cards.text: But say the spot is white, it doesn't look deeper than the skin, and the hair hasn't turned white. Now it's a maybe.

cards.question: When it's a maybe, the priest isolates the person for ___ days.

cards.text: Day seven, the priest takes another look. The spot hasn't changed. It hasn't spread. It's just... sitting there.

cards.question: Since the spot didn't change or spread in seven days, the priest sends the person home clean right then.

cards.text: Nope. Another seven days. Friend, I spent years in a junk drawer, so I know waiting. But two weeks staring at one spot on your arm? I'd be checking it every five minutes like a phone with no bars!

cards.question: On the second checkup, the sore has faded and hasn't spread. The priest pronounces the person ___. It's a rash.
Once the priest pronounces the person clean after the rash, the person must wash their ___.

cards.text: But if the rash spreads after the person has shown themselves to the priest for cleansing, it's right back to the priest. Like paying off the car and the check-engine light comes on the next morning.

cards.question: The priest looks again and sees the rash has spread on the skin. What does he say it is?

cards.text: Next case. Someone's brought in with a white swelling that has turned the hair white, and there's raw flesh in the swelling.

cards.question: With raw flesh in a white swelling, the priest still isolates the person for seven days before deciding.

cards.text: Then a surprise. The disease breaks out over all the person's skin, from head to foot, as far as the priest can see. I'm holding my breath on my gold base, friend.

cards.question: The disease has covered the person's entire body, and it has all turned white. What does the priest pronounce?

answers.text: The person must wait a week

cards.text: WAIT. Head to foot, and it's CLEAN? But whenever raw flesh shows up, the priest pronounces the person unclean. The raw flesh is unclean.

cards.question: Later the raw flesh changes and turns white, so the person goes back to the priest. Remembering the head-to-foot case, what does the priest pronounce?

answers.text: The person must leave the camp

cards.text: Now a boil heals. Great news! Then a white swelling or a reddish-white spot shows up right where the boil was, so it's off to the priest.

cards.question: Same checkup as before. Which two signs make the priest pronounce the person unclean?

answers.text: Beneath the skin with white hair

cards.text: If there's no white hair, it's not beneath the skin and it has faded, that's seven days apart. If it spreads, it's an infection, and the person is unclean.

cards.question: But if the spot after the boil stays the same and doesn't spread, it's only the ___ from the boil.

cards.text: Then a burn whose raw area turns reddish-white or white gets the same checkup. White hair and deeper than the skin means unclean. If it fades and doesn't spread after seven days, it's only the scar from the burn. Same recipe, different batch.
Now a man or a woman has an infection on the head or chin. New spot, new rule. This time the priest is watching for a different color of hair.

cards.question: On the head or chin, the spot looks deeper than the skin. What kind of hair in it means the person is unclean?

cards.text: If it's not deeper than the skin and there's no black hair, it's seven days apart. Day seven, it hasn't spread, there's no yellow hair, and it's still not deeper than the skin.

cards.question: Before another seven days apart, what does the person with the scaly spot have to do?

answers.text: Shave except for the scaly area
Cover the area with a cloth
Wash the area in running water

cards.text: Week two. It hasn't spread, and it's not deeper than the skin. The priest pronounces the person clean, and they wash their clothes. Somebody cue the music!

cards.question: If the scaly outbreak spreads after the person's cleansing, the priest still has to find yellow hair before pronouncing them unclean.
Instead, the priest sees the scaly outbreak is unchanged and black hair has grown in it. What does that mean?

cards.text: Then a man or a woman has white spots on the skin. The priest looks at just what kind of white they are.

cards.question: If the white spots are dull white, it's a ___ rash, and the person is clean.
If a man loses his hair and goes bald, or his hairline recedes, he becomes unclean.

cards.text: But a reddish-white sore on the bald head or forehead is a different story. If the swelling looks like a skin disease, the priest pronounces him unclean.
Now the hard part: how a diseased person has to live. They wear torn clothes and let their hair hang loose.

cards.question: As a diseased person cries out, 'Unclean, unclean!' what must they cover?
As long as a person has the infection, they remain unclean. Where must they live?

cards.text: Then the LORD turns from skin to stuff. Wool or linen, a weave or a knit, anything made of leather. If a certain mark shows up, it's mildew, and it goes to the priest. That's right, friend. The priest checks your clothes too.

cards.question: If the mark in the fabric or leather is ___ or ___, it's mildew and must be shown to the priest.
The priest examines the mildewed item. Just like with a spot on the skin, what does he do first?

answers.text: Hand it back to the owner

cards.text: Day seven. The mildew has spread. It doesn't matter how the item is used. It's a harmful mildew, and the article is unclean.

cards.question: The mildew in the item has spread and it's harmful. What happens to the item?

answers.text: It is buried outside the camp
It is kept by the priest

cards.text: But if the mildew hasn't spread, the priest orders the item washed and set apart for another seven days. The good old 'let it soak and see' method. I've done that with a baking sheet more times than I can count.

cards.question: After washing, the mildew hasn't spread but it looks exactly the same. Since it didn't spread, the item is clean.

cards.text: Now say the mildew has faded after washing. The priest cuts the contaminated section right out of the fabric or leather. Snip.

cards.question: The priest cut the mildewed section out, but the mildew shows up again in the item. What must be done?
If the mildew disappears from an item after washing, the item is washed again, and it will be clean.

cards.text: And that's the law for mildew in wool, linen and leather, for pronouncing it clean or unclean. We'll leave it there for now, friend. But the teaching on clean and unclean isn't done yet.

findings.problem: The opening card has 4 sentences: 'Then the LORD speaks…', 'He's laying out…', 'No doctor's office here, friend.' and 'That person gets brought…'. The limit for the opening card is 3.

rule.text: The opening card can be up to 3 sentences. It says who is speaking, to whom, and what is going on.

findings.problem: Several story cards that aren't long-stretch summaries run past 2 sentences. Stop 1 card 6 has 4 ('Day seven…', 'The spot hasn't changed.', 'It hasn't spread.', 'It's just... sitting there.'). Stop 1 card 8 has 4. Stop 1 card 15 has 3. Stop 1 card 17 has 4. Stop 2 card 1 has 3. Stop 2 card 6 has 3. Stop 2 card 10 has 4. Stop 3 card 1 has 4. Stop 3 card 4 has 4. Stop 3 card 6 has 3. Stop 3 card 8 has 3.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The card cites Leviticus 13:5-6, but it only tells the second seven-day isolation from 13:5. Nothing from 13:6 is on this card. Card 9 asks about 13:6.

rule.text: Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: Leviticus 13:11 calls the white swelling with raw flesh a chronic skin disease and says the priest pronounces the person unclean. No card ever states this verdict. The true/false card only shows that there is no isolation, so the baker leaves without the outcome of this case.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.

findings.problem: 'Then a surprise.' signals the verdict before card 16 asks for it. Every disease case so far ended in 'unclean', so calling the result a surprise points the baker to 'The person is clean' and rules out the other answers.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: The wrong answer 'Redness with swelling' is too close to the passage. In 13:19 a white swelling or reddish-white spot is what sends the person to the priest. In 13:42-44 a reddish-white swelling makes a man unclean. A baker could argue it's right. The right answer is also about twice as long as the wrong answers, so it stands out.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: The card cites Leviticus 13:35-36. The right answer (False: the priest need not look for yellow hair) comes only from 13:36. Verse 35 is just the setup. Stop 1 card 18 handles this correctly by citing only 13:17.

rule.text: A choice card cites only the verses of its right answer.

findings.problem: Stop 2 is mostly a straight run through the rules with very little humor. The only lighter lines are 'Great news!', 'Same recipe, different batch.' and 'Somebody cue the music!'. Those read as mildly pleasant, not laugh-out-loud, across 19 cards.

rule.text: But he is FUNNY. Not mildly amusing. Laugh-out-loud funny, the kind a baker repeats to a friend. … If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.

findings.problem: Leviticus 13 is almost entirely case-by-case rules. That looks like the 'long stretch' categories ('rules for everyday life', 'repeated reports'), which get one summary card and no choice cards. But the stretch is the whole passage, and 'a stretch never gets a stop of its own.' The walkthrough handles this inconsistently. The burn case (13:24-28) is summarized on one card as a stretch, while the nearly identical boil case (13:18-23) and the head/chin case get several choice cards.
findings.question: When a whole passage is made of detailed rules, should it be walked through with choice cards case by case, treated as long stretches, or a mix? If a mix, which repeated cases (like the burn after the boil) should be summarized instead of asked about?
